title: The sacred vessel
hookLine: the world is a sacred vessel; try to seize it and you ruin it (Tao Te Ching 29)
last: KNOW STRENGTH, KEEP TO THE SOFT, BE THE VALLEY.

cards: A little kid with a bubble wand on a summer porch. One long breath, and out floats a bubble the size of a melon, wobbling, shining, turning colors. The kid is thrilled.
And then does the obvious thing: reaches out with both hands to catch it. Pop. A wet spot on the palms, and a stunned face.
Try again. Pop. The only way to keep watching the bubble is to leave it alone.
Chapter twenty-nine of the Tao Te Ching says the whole world is like that bubble, and it says so to people who want to run things.

teach.b: First, trying to take the world. The chapter starts with someone who wants to take hold of the world and do something with it, fix it, run it, improve it. The speaker says plainly: I see that it can't be done.
Second, a sacred vessel. Then the reason. The world, the chapter says, is a sacred vessel, a spirit-like thing.
It can't be acted upon that way. In Legge's translation: "He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it." Grab it and you break it.
Clutch it and it slips away. A vessel is a container, a made thing. Call it sacred, and it becomes something you handle carefully, with both hands, never roughly.
Third, some lead, some follow. Next comes a list of how things actually are. Some go ahead, and some follow behind.
Some breathe out warm, and some breathe out cold. Some are strong, some are weak. Some are up, some are down.
The world has its own rhythms, its own back and forth, and a grabbing hand can't flatten them into one straight line.
Fourth, no excess, no extremes. So what does the sage do?

teach.h: HOLD IT IN YOUR GRASP, AND LOSE IT.
teach.b: The chapter's answer is short: the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive. Not nothing. Not passivity.
Just no overreach. Like the kid on the porch, learning, bubble after bubble, that the best way to keep the shining thing is to stand back and breathe.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-nine as a caution against overreach: they work toward what they want while letting go of control over how it turns out.

o: a jar that holds the sage's secret teachings
the world, which breaks when you try to grab it
a temple cup used only by priests and kings

s: chapter twenty-nine says a strong enough ruler can take the world and improve it
the speaker says it can't be done: the world is a sacred vessel, and grabbing it destroys it.
the chapter lists how things differ: some lead, some follow, some strong, some weak
the world has its own back and forth, which a grabbing hand can't flatten.
the chapter tells the sage to do nothing at all
it says the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive: no overreach, not no action.

games.q: you've been handed the chance to take hold of the world and fix it your way. chapter twenty-nine is open in front of you. what does it say?
o: grab it firmly, and set it straight.
it can't be done: grab it and you destroy it.
take half, and leave the rest.
games.why: "he who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it." the world is a sacred vessel.

practice: Open your hands on your lap, palms up. Bring to mind one thing you're trying hard to make happen, and feel where your mind is gripping it.
Without giving up on it, loosen the grip the way your hands are open now, and let it float like that bubble: still wanted, no longer squeezed.

wordCard.voice: The sacred vessel. Chapter twenty-nine's name for the world: a spirit-like thing that breaks when grabbed and slips away when clutched. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, tiānxià shénqì: all under heaven is a sacred vessel, from Tao Te Ching 29.

carryVoice: Your line: don't grab it. The world is a thing for careful hands. Back tomorrow, same hill.
